title: The guests and Lut
hookLine: the angels visit Ibrahim, then Lut's city is overturned (11:69–83)

lines: THE SAME GUESTS, ON THE ROAD.
cards: Last year you sat in Ibrahim's tent when the strangers came: the roasted calf, the hands that didn't reach for it, the laugh at the news of a son. Surah Hud follows those same guests out of the tent and down the road.
Before they go, Ibrahim does something this path skipped then. He argues with them. He pleads for the people of the city they're heading to.
Then the guests arrive at a second door, in that city, at dusk. And the man who opens it is filled with dread.

teach.b: First, the pleading. Verse seventy-four says Ibrahim began to plead with God for the people of Lut, and verse seventy-five explains why: Ibrahim was forbearing, tender-hearted, always turning to God.

The answer comes gently: Ibrahim, leave this; the command has come. Now the second door. The guests reach Lut's house, and verse seventy-seven says he was troubled for them, his heart tight: this is a hard day.

He knows his city. Soon the men come rushing to his door, wanting his guests. The Qur'an names this city's wrongs in several surahs; in this telling, the heart of it is a crowd coming to seize a man's guests.

teach.h: DON'T SHAME ME IN MY GUESTS.
teach.b: Lut stands in his doorway and pleads: fear God, and don't shame me in my guests. Isn't there one right-minded man among you? There isn't.

teach.h: IF ONLY I HAD A STRONG SUPPORT.
teach.b: And Lut says something painfully honest, in verse eighty: if only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in some strong support. A host, alone, with nothing to protect his guests but his own body in the doorway.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ later said, in a hadith in Bukhari: may God have mercy on Lut; he was taking refuge in a strong support. He was, though he couldn't see it.
The guests tell him: we are messengers from your Lord; they will not reach you.

teach.h: LEAVE BY NIGHT; DON'T LOOK BACK.
teach.b: Leave in the last part of the night, and let no one look back, except your wife. At dawn the city is overturned. Two hosts: one fed strangers before he knew them; one stood in the door for them.

how: Muslim teachers speak of hospitality to guests as part of faith, citing Ibrahim's welcome and Lut's protection of his guests, and the hadith 'whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest' (Sahih al-Bukhari).

o: the angel sent to warn the city at dusk
the prophet who guarded his guests in his doorway
the prophet who pleaded with God for the city

games.q: two hosts, one set of guests — tap the pairs.
p: pleaded for the people of Lut
stood in the doorway for his guests

s: Ibrahim pleaded for the people of Lut
11:74–75: he pleaded with God, forbearing and tender-hearted, and was told the command had come.
Lut had the strength to protect his guests
he said: if only I had strength against you, or a strong support to turn to.
his wife stayed behind and shared the city's fate.

games.q: you're Lut. the men of the city are at your door, demanding your guests. what do you do?
o: hand them over to save yourself.
stand in the door: don't shame me in my guests.
climb out the back and run.
games.why: he pleaded: fear God, don't shame me in my guests; isn't there one right-minded man among you? then the guests revealed themselves as angels.

practice: Think of someone who is new around you: a new coworker, a family just moved in, a student far from home, a person at the mosque or the bus stop you've never spoken to.

Picture greeting them with peace, simply and without suspicion, in a public place where you both feel safe, and what you could offer: a name, a seat, a cup of tea. If you pray, you can ask good for them.

wordCard.voice: Lut. The prophet who stood in his doorway to guard the angels sent as his guests, before his city was overturned. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "my guests," from Lut's plea in 11:78: don't shame me in my guests.

carryVoice: Your line: hospitality protects. Two hosts, and a welcome that became a shelter. Until tomorrow.
